😎 Plus: South Carolina gets a dose of Trump

It’s Friday. Against all odds and several hundred emails, we’ve made it.

 

In today’s issue:

  • Beef tariffs get a timeout

  • Bessent weighs America’s debt

  • Trump goes all in for Graham

  • IndyCar zooms into DC

Programming note: Hello! We are Colin Meyn and Steff Danielle Thomas filling in for Cate. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to cmeyn@thehill.com or sthomas@thehill.com.

 

💵 ON THE ECONOMY

This moo-ve is not going to thrill cattle farmers:

© AP

President Trump is intervening in the beef markets in a move certain to irk some key constituencies. 

What’s the deal? In a Truth Social post, Trump said, “for the next 90 days, the United States will allow up to 300,000 metric tons of product for ground beef to be imported with no out of quota tariff. We have a commitment that this beef will be sold at 25 percent below current market prices.”

The president did not say where the beef is coming from, but he has previously considered similar arrangements with Argentina. 

Beef prices have risen faster than other foods during Trump’s second term. Both ground beef and beef steak pieces rose by 9 percent or more year-on-year, according to the July CPI report.

Queue the blowback: Trump’s previous meddling in the beef market has drawn criticism from cattle ranchers and Republican senators in major beef-producing states. 

Sen. Tim Sheehy (R-Mont.), a staunch Trump ally, said Friday in a post on social platform X that he’d been warning against such action “because American ranchers have been struggling against the packer monopoly for decades, and this will further harm them — most of whom are MAGA Republicans.”

Other criticism came from some predictable figures. 

“What a slap in the face to American cattlemen & consumers,” Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) wrote online. “Worse than socialism! Dumping foreign beef in U.S. markets can temporarily lower prices but it won’t incentivize American farmers to raise more beef.”

Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) chimed in too, saying U.S. farmers will now “be undercut by foreign imported beef, as they have been hit financially with high cost of fertilizer and diesel from Trump’s war with Iran.”

Bessent is busy putting out another fire:

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is scrambling to convince the markets to stop selling off U.S. bonds. 

He moved on Wednesday to double the Treasury’s buyback limit, and on Thursday went on CNBC to declare he was ready to intervene further if needed. 

But bond yields only moved higher Thursday, after ticking down Wednesday. The 30-year bond yield, a key indicator of economic health, remained above 5.25 percent on Friday, as high as it’s been since before the global recession in 2008. 

Tell me more about this bond yield: Sure. It’s basically how much interest the government has to pay on future bonds it issues. When investors are feeling good about the economy, yields are low because demand is high. When investors are feeling anxious, yields go up to help them hedge against risk.

Bessent told CNBC he’s got more tricks up his sleeve while arguing the markets are misreading America’s economic strength. 

“We have a big toolkit,” the Treasury chief said. “Part of it is signaling here and to show that we believe that the yields don’t reflect the underlying fundamentals.”

Read more from CNBC on what he could actually do about it. 

The Hill’s very own Niall Stanage offers a helpful explainer on this whole situation. 

 

🗳️ ON THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL

Trump to throw Graham a lifeline:

Trump is headed tonight to Myrtle Beach with a mission: Give Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) one last push before Tuesday’s GOP runoff against Rep. Ralph Norman. Graham is serving out her late brother Lindsey Graham’s term, but keeping the seat is proving a little trickier than stepping into it.

Graham had a particularly bumpy night on the debate stage earlier this week, admitting national security is “not” her thing when pressed about Taiwan and the South China Sea. Norman and his allies wasted no time jumping on the flub, while the senator has tried to turn it into an outsider pitch: She’s new to politics, and she’s not pretending otherwise.

Can Trump help close the deal?: Myrtle Beach is a smart place to try. It’s the heart of Rep. Russell Fry’s (R-S.C.) district, putting a potentially crucial pool of GOP voters up for grabs — and the president’s endorsement power back in the spotlight. 

💬 Follow today’s live blog

 

➤ S’MORE FUEL FOR THE FIRE:

The debate gaffe gave critics plenty of ammunition. 

Former UN Ambassador Nikki Haley said national security knowledge isn’t “something you inherit,” while former South Carolina state Rep. Adam Morgan called it a “stunning debate flop.”

Former Rep. Katie Porter (D-Calif.) was even more cutting: “This might be just dumb.”

 

➤ TRUMP CARD:

Trump knows how to appeal to Palmetto State voters.

In 2024, he handily beat Haley, the state’s former governor, in the GOP presidential primary before carrying South Carolina by nearly 18 points in the general election.

That history could give Graham a much-needed edge Tuesday. Former White House chief of staff Mick Mulvaney recently told The Hill that without the president’s backing, she “wouldn’t have a chance.”

 

➤ NORMAN NOTCHES SUPPORT:

Pick a side: Former GOP Rep. Mark Sanford, who threw his hat into the ring for Graham’s seat, said Friday he’ll be voting for Norman.

(You might remember him from another story line…)

Rogers pitches a data center gap year:

Michigan GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers is reaching for the pause button on the state’s data center boom. 

The former lawmaker called for a one-year moratorium on construction of the data centers while Michiganders get answers about energy costs, water use and the approval process.

It’s also becoming a dividing line with his opponent, progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D). Rogers wants decisions kept closer to home, while El-Sayed is pushing for federal guardrails on the projects.

The data center debate is heating up elsewhere, too:. In Ohio, former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) is using the issue to go after GOP Sen. Jon Husted in another marquee Senate race.

Republicans have gotten the message. The National Republican Senatorial Committee is also paying attention. The Senate GOP campaign arm recently warned AI companies to make their case — and fast — about who benefits from all that new infrastructure and who gets stuck with the bill.

 

➤ ROGERS HAS GROUND TO MAKE UP:

Speaking of data, Rogers has some other numbers to worry about. 

Two recent polls from AARP and Susquehanna Polling & Research show El-Sayed leading the Republican in the race.

There’s still plenty of time to close the gap, though. Cook Political Report rates the contest a “toss-up.”
 

🏁 OTHER NEWS:

This is gonna be kinda crazy:

Downtown Washington, D.C., is going to become an IndyCar circuit this weekend. We’ve known this is coming for a while … but it’s getting real around here. 

IndyCar President Doug Boles casually told Newsmax on Thursday there “could be a little carnage” on some of the sharper turns in the course. 

Race cars will reach speeds of some 180 mph as they whip past landmarks like the National Archives, National Gallery of Art and Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum. 

Take the Metro! More than 200,000 people are expected on the National Mall for the event, with much of downtown shut down to traffic. The race is 147 laps. Yeah, we thought the same thing with the “47,” but it’s actually a 250-mile race to honor the semi-quincentennial.

Read more: Getting ready for this race took a lot of work, as this story in The Athletic lays out.

 

➤ QUICK HITS:

— 🤝 Trump is looking to rekindle his first-term bromance with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un, but Kim hasn’t exactly been rushing to meet him halfway. Experts warn another meeting between the leaders could come at a cost.

— 🥊 Massachusetts Rep. Seth Moulton and incumbent Sen. Ed Markey came out swinging in their final Democratic Senate primary debate Thursday. Moulton pushed his case for generational change, while Markey defended his progressive record. 📖Read the takeaways here.

— ⚓ The USS George Washington arrived in the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln after its lengthy deployment drew scrutiny over supply shortages and sailors’ mental health. 

— 📻 Trump and his former fixer-turned-enemy Michael Cohen appear to have turned over a new leaf. The president said he respects Cohen for taking back things he previously said about him as the two reunited for a radio interview. Click here for more details. 

 

➤ MORE READS:

The New York Times: Trump Administration Has a Different Way to Drain Harvard Funding

Politico: Gavin Newsom’s unfinished wildfire business

The Wall Street Journal: ‘Ghost Job’ Ads Are Getting So Bad That Lawmakers Want to Ban Them

The Associated Press: What’s in a name? Why naming storms, military operations and medical maladies matters

🗓️ COMING UP

The House and Senate are out. President Trump is in Washington for meetings then will travel later Friday to South Carolina. (All times EDT)

 

2 p.m.: Trump participates in a policy meeting.

7 p.m. Trump campaigns in Myrtle Beach, S.C., for Darline Graham.

SATURDAY: Trump has executive time and then attends a MAGA Inc. meeting.

SUNDAY: The president and first lady Melania Trump will attend the Freedom 250 Grand Prix on the National Mall.

🐝 INTERNET BUZZ

👵Celebrate: Today is National Senior Citizens Day! Make sure to give a call to your grandparents today! Or your siblings for a good ruse.

 

📱 Scroll patrol: Could a courtroom cure doomscrolling? Meta is on trial over claims Instagram and Facebook were designed to keep young users hooked. Here’s what it could mean for your feed.

 

👋 AND FINALLY…

Another busy week in the books — and sometimes you just need to slow things down and read to your chocolate lab. It’s called balance.

data.title: Watch live: Vance seeks to sell Trump agenda to Ohio voters
data.description:
Vice President Vance is heading back to his Ohio hometown on Friday afternoon, as he looks to sell President Trump’s economic agenda to voters ahead of the November midterms.

Vance will deliver remarks at Cleveland-Cliffs Middletown Works, a steel plant where his grandfather worked for nearly four decades. He is expected to tout the administration’s efforts to boost domestic manufacturing and will be joined by Energy Secretary Chris Wright.

The stop comes as Republicans face increasingly competitive races in the Buckeye State. Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), who was appointed to fill Vance’s former Senate seat, is facing former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), while Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is running against Democrat Amy Acton for governor.

The event in Middletown, Ohio. is scheduled to begin at 1 p.m. EDT.

Watch the live video above.

data.title: 'Who knows?': Jill Biden responds to theory Joe Biden was drugged before debate
data.description:
Everyone remembers that disastrous presidential debate then President Biden had against Donald Trump in 2024. It was so jarring that it ultimately helped end his reelection campaign. And now, nearly two years later, former first lady Jill Biden is once again talking about what happened that night — including whether her husband could have been drugged.  

She made the comments during an appearance on “The Jamie Kern Lima Show.” Asked if he was “having a stroke or — uh, uh, was he drugged? Were there any steps taken after to rule out?” Jill Biden answered, “Oh, yeah. Either.”

“I mean, Joe and I both had a team of doctors around both of us at all times, and he had a team, I had a team. … And yeah, they checked him out. I mean, once we got off the stage, I went to the green room to get my, my pocketbook and all that stuff, and he went to his staff and the docs and, um, and they said, ‘Jill, he’s fine. He’s OK.’”  

So here’s where I think we need to separate what we know from what we still don’t know.  

We know Joe Biden had an extraordinarily poor debate performance. We know Jill Biden says she immediately noticed that he did not seem like himself. And we know his doctors examined him afterward, according to her, and told her he was OK.  

What we do not have is evidence that Joe Biden was drugged. But when asked about the possibility that someone could have put something in his drink, she said, “Who knows? Who knows?”  

And that’s the problem with continuing to elevate that possibility: “Who knows?” is not evidence.

In her memoir, “View from the East Wing,” Jill Biden herself describes the fear and confusion she felt watching the debate. She wrote that she wondered, “Is this a stroke?” and even asked herself, “Has he been drugged?” She has said she still doesn’t know what happened that night.

Joe Biden was 81 years old. The debate intensified already existing concerns about his age and ability to serve another four years. He ultimately ended his reelection campaign less than a month later.  

The Democratic Party has to be honest. There have been serious questions about whether Biden’s age and health were adequately confronted inside his political circle. The 2025 book “Original Sin,” by Jake Tapper and Alex Thompson, argued that Biden’s inner circle shielded him from difficult information and that concerns about his decline were minimized. The first lady is depicted as a central figure in hiding that from public view.  

So I don’t think the lesson here is that Jill Biden should never talk about her husband’s presidency. She absolutely has a right to tell her story. But you cannot rewrite history, no matter how many times you try.  

And nearly two years later, the Democratic Party still has to reckon with the consequences of that debate — not because Trump needs another villain, and not because Joe Biden needs another defense, but because voters deserve political leaders who can acknowledge what went wrong without searching for a mystery explanation that has never been substantiated.  

Joe Biden is now battling stage 4 prostate cancer that has spread to his bones, according to his son. Jill Biden has spoken publicly about the toll that diagnosis has taken on their family and about trying to make the most of the time they have together. One way to help both Biden’s legacy and Democrats’ future chances is to stop pretending and stop relitigating the past. At that point, the party may learn from it and finally be able to move forward. 

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

data.title: Pentagon says over 750 US service members wounded in Iran war
data.description:
The Pentagon said that over 750 U.S. service members have been wounded since the U.S. war against Iran began in late February. 

The department updated its war casualty database this week with another 50 injured service members. 

When totals from the Operation Epic Fury rubric are combined with updated figures in the “Overseas Operations” category, the total number comes out to 756 wounded in action, according to the Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) data. 

Last month, the Pentagon formed the “Overseas Operations” section for casualties in the conflict “starting” July 7, the same day that the U.S. military resumed airstrikes against Iran in light of Tehran’s forces targeting shipping tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. 

President Trump notified Congress that week of the resumption of hostilities, giving the U.S. forces in the U.S. Central Command theater another 60 days of ability to conduct kinetic action with congressional approval. 

The Pentagon has previously come under fire from news media outlets and Democratic lawmakers after the number of U.S. service members killed and injured in action went down in the DCAS database. 

The updated figures also come as Trump announced earlier this week that the U.S. is launching the “MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER” against Iran amid the apparently stalled talks between Iran and Oman to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. 

“This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale,” the president said on Wednesday.

data.title: Massie, Greene slam Trump's move to lower beef prices
data.description:
Two Republicans pushed back on the Trump administration’s Friday decision to temporarily lift certain tariffs on imported ground beef in an effort to bring down prices for American consumers ahead of the midterm elections. 

President Trump announced in a Truth Social post on Friday morning that he had finalized “a deal to substantially lower the price of ground beef for working American families.”

The president said his administration will allow up to 300,000 metric tons of ground beef to be imported without an “out-of-quota tariff” in the next 90 days. 

The imported product would be sold at 25 percent below market price — a move Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie (R) called a “slap in the face to American cattlemen & consumers.”

“Worse than socialism! Dumping foreign beef in U.S. markets can temporarily lower prices but it won’t incentivize American farmers to raise more beef,” Massie wrote on social media. 

The GOP lawmaker urged the Trump administration to bring back labels indicating which products countries were imported from and called on Congress to pass his Processing Revival and Intrastate Meat Exemption (PRIME) Act. 

The PRIME Act would permit states to allow farmers and ranchers to slaughter their livestock at local slaughterhouses and reduce reliance on the select meat processing centers approved by the U.S. Department of Agriculture. 

Former GOP Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (Ga.) also joined in on criticizing this move, accusing the Trump administration of “making it even harder for American beef ranchers and producers.”

“Now they will be undercut by foreign imported beef, as they have been hit financially with high cost of fertilizer and diesel from Trump’s war with Iran,” Greene wrote in a Friday social media post. “The Trump admins attempt to lower the cost of beef is American beef LAST and foreign beef FIRST.”

A historically-small U.S. cattle herd and high consumer demand has driven up the domestic cost of ground beef. 

The average price of 100 percent ground beef per pound was around $6.89 in July — an over 10 percent increase from a year ago, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data shared by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. 

Trump said on Friday this new move will “reduce prices for Americans while giving space for our Great American Beef Herd to grow again.”

data.title: Building families shouldn't be this hard
data.description:
The deeply personal decision of when and how to build a family has suddenly become part of a national conversation. At the heart of this conversation is the profound hope held by millions of Americans: to one day hold one’s own child for the first time.

For each of us, that moment came after years of uncertainty, hope, and extraordinary help from others. Our paths were different, but they led to the same realization: You are not free if you don’t have the freedom to decide when and how to have a family.

One of us welcomed a son after doctors said there was only a one-in-a-million chance of conceiving without in vitro fertilization. The other became a father to two children through surrogacy after nearly three years of navigating the financial, legal and emotional complexities of the process.

Those experiences changed us and made one thing abundantly clear: For too many Americans, becoming a parent is far more difficult than it should be.

No one should have to win the financial or legal lottery to become a parent. Yet today’s system is too often defined by staggering costs, outdated policies and unnecessary legal uncertainty. Families and same-sex couples spend years navigating barriers that have little to do with medicine and everything to do with bureaucracy or politics. That should change.

If we are serious about strengthening families, growing our economy, and investing in the next generation, we should be making it easier for Americans to become parents.

This is not a Democratic issue or a Republican issue, it’s an American one. When Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) shared her experience navigating the costly and complicated fertility care system, the response cut across the usual dividing lines with praise from conservative and progressive media personalities. As a nation, we disagree on many things. But we agree that having a family is a gift and a right, and our system should make it both accessible and affordable for all.

Fortunately, the solutions don’t require reinventing the system. They require modernizing it. Congress and the administration should focus on three practical reforms.

First, make fertility-related expenses — including in-vitro fertilization and surrogacy — fully tax deductible for all Americans seeking to start a family. Families routinely spend tens or even hundreds of thousands of dollars pursuing parenthood. Those costs should be treated like the essential medical and family-building expenses they are.

Second, modernize federal insurance rules so that employers can more easily offer comprehensive fertility and surrogacy benefits. While some insurance plans cover portions of IVF, coverage for the medical care associated with surrogacy remains inconsistent or nonexistent.

Updating federal guidance would give employers greater flexibility to support employees who rely on assisted reproductive technology to build their families. One of us runs a company whose employees are eligible for up to $300,000 in family formation support that can go towards IVF, surrogacy and adoption. Public policy should make it easier for other employers to follow suit.

Third, states should follow Colorado’s lead and pass clear parentage laws, including orders that let intended parents establish their legal rights before the baby is even born. That way, when a child arrives, there is no question about who his or her legal parents are. No family should begin one of its happiest days facing avoidable legal confusion.

Federal policy should also adopt the modern medical definition of infertility that recognizes infertility is not defined solely by months of unsuccessful attempts to conceive, but by a person’s inability to achieve a successful pregnancy based on their full medical, sexual and reproductive history. That would ensure today’s policies reflect today’s science and today’s families.

These ideas are already gaining traction across the country.

Colorado and California have demonstrated that thoughtful reforms can expand access to fertility care while supporting families. George was proud to support California’s landmark expansion of in vitro insurance coverage, and employers are increasingly recognizing that helping employees build families is both good policy and good business. 

Like all Americans, our stories are different. Our politics are not identical. But parenthood has a way of clarifying priorities. Every parent who dreams of raising a child should have a fair opportunity to pursue that dream.

This should not be controversial. It should be one of the easiest decisions we make for a better America.

George Arison is chairman and CEO of Grindr Inc. John Hickenlooper (D) is a father to two sons and the junior U.S. senator from Colorado.

data.title: ICE begins deporting Haitians who lost temporary protections
data.description:
The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) carried out its first deportation flight to Haiti on Thursday since the Trump administration terminated deportation protections for hundreds of thousands of Haitians earlier this year.

The plane, which carried over 160 people, arrived in the northern Haitian city of Cap-Haitien, The Associated Press reported. The U.S. currently has a ban in place on flights in and out of the country’s main airport in the capital city of Port-au-Prince due to ongoing gang violence. 

The deportees on this flight included those previously covered under Temporary Protected Status (TPS), a U.S. program that protects from deportation foreign nationals who cannot safely return to their home country and offers them a pathway to work authorization. 

The Supreme Court ruled in June that the Trump administration could end this protection for the around 330,000 Haitians and over 6,000 Syrians covered by this program. 

The administration has looked to terminate deportation protections for migrants from 13 of the 17 countries covered by TPS, arguing that these countries no longer meet the required criteria. 

The State Department still lists Haiti as a “Level 4: Do Not Travel” country on its travel advisory website, citing gang-related crime, terrorism, unrest and limited healthcare services in the nation. The department also notes that Haiti has been under a national state of emergency since 2024. 

Immigration activist groups have warned that people deported to Haiti could face dangerous conditions in the country. The U.N. reported that more than 3,100 people were reported killed and 1,189 others were injured from January to June of this year.

Haiti’s Group Supporting Refugees and Returnees warned in a Thursday statement the country was “not ready to receive this number of migrants who were in the TPS program.”

data.title: What Trump's cold shoulder toward South Korea means to our allies
data.description:
President Trump’s decision to cut roughly in half the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises with South Korea, along with his desire for a fourth meeting with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un, has caused considerable consternation among Washington’s key allies in the Far East.

On a visit to Australia, Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi indirectly reflected his unease with Trump’s decision when he stated, “As Japan faces the most severe and complicated security environment in the postwar era, the cooperation among Japan, the U.S. and South Korea is critical to the peace and stability of the region.”

Koizumi’s response to Trump’s action repeated almost verbatim the words of his introduction to the 2026 white paper “Defense of Japan,” in which he added, “In the Indo-Pacific, not only are China and North Korea further strengthening their military capabilities, China-Russia and Russia-North Korea are also reinforcing their cooperation.”

The white paper also stated that “North Korea’s military activities pose an even more grave and imminent threat to Japan’s national security than ever before.”

Koizumi’s Australian host, Richard Marles, said much the same thing, leaving no doubt that Australia has a starkly different view of North Korea from Trump’s. He observed that Canberra “is very concerned about North Korea’s nuclear program as well as its missile program, and we have consistently made that point.” And he termed South Korea “a critically important country,” for his country and for the trilateral relationship among Australia, Japan and South Korea.  

Left unstated on the part of both defense ministers was a concern about America’s reliability as an ally. The announcement of the cutback in the U.S.-South Korean exercises follows the redeployment of the aircraft carrier USS George Washington from the Western Pacific to the Middle East, leaving East Asia without an American aircraft carrier presence for the second time since 2024, when the carrier USS Abraham Lincoln and its battle group first joined the battle group that had already been on station in the Middle East.

With no end in sight to the Iran war, it remains unclear how long there will be no carrier deployed in East Asia. Moreover, it appears that while officially assigning highest priority to East Asia after defense of the American homeland, the redeployment of the carrier to the Middle East is a sign that Washington’s priorities on paper do not match its actual concerns. 

China has officially taken a nuanced position regarding the cutback in the joint U.S.-South Korean exercises as well as Trump’s desire to meet yet again with Kim. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jiang simply stated that “maintaining peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula and advancing the political settlement of the Korean Peninsula issue serve the common interests of all parties.” Yet surely not coincidentally, only days after Trump’s announcement, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi was to make his first visit to Seoul in five years.

Beijing cannot but view Trump’s announcement with some satisfaction. Indeed, China’s state run media have been considerably less circumspect than the government itself about Trump’s decision reflecting his unhappiness with Seoul’s refusal to support actively the U.S. operation against Iran. The Xinhua News Agency asserted that this is “a stock method the U.S. government uses when pressuring allies … [that] reveals US frustration resulting from policy deadlock on the Korean Peninsula and over Iran.” Xinhua added that “such an alliance system is bound to continuously erode and gradually head toward disintegration.”

China’s view that the American alliance system is beginning to fray is likely premature, but it does have some basis in current reality. Trump’s dissatisfaction with South Korea — and with Japan, for that matter — mirrors his unhappiness with America’s NATO allies. His tariff policy and complaints that European and East Asian allies had not committed sufficient resources for defense preceded the onset of the American operations in the Middle East.

To these prior complaints, Trump has now added criticism of the allies for not actively supporting the ongoing Iran operation.

Trump may rightly feel that any understanding he reaches with Kim will reduce tensions on the Korean Peninsula and in East Asia more generally. But coupling his desire to meet the North Korean dictator again with the cutback in joint exercises with South Korea sends the wrong message both to America’s allies and to Beijing — and Russia, for that matter, which has also become a major Japanese concern.

Even if the current exercises remain truncated, Trump could still elect to let future exercises run their planned course. This would not only reassure nervous allies but also strengthen his hand if his meeting with Kim actually were to take place.

Dov S. Zakheim is a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and vice chairman of the board for the Foreign Policy Research Institute. He was undersecretary of Defense (comptroller) and chief financial officer for the Department of Defense from 2001 to 2004 and a deputy undersecretary of Defense from 1985 to 1987.

data.title: Trump temporarily lifts ground beef import tariffs
data.description:
President Trump announced Friday that the U.S. will pause higher tariffs on ground beef imports for 90 days to lower costs of the meat for consumers.

Trump, in a post on Truth Social, said the U.S. will allow up to 300,000 metric tons of ground beef to be imported without an “out-of-quota tariff,” or the higher rate often placed on imported goods when the trade volume surpasses a certain threshold.

He added that the administration is doing this “as we work to rebuild this herd and help our ranchers.”

The move will likely anger the cattle industry as more imported beef makes its way into the country.

Trump said Friday that the price of beef “soared at their fastest rate and the American beef herd fell to its smallest size in modern history” under the Biden administration.

“We have a commitment that this beef will be sold at 25 percent below current market prices,” the president continued. “This deal will reduce prices for Americans while giving space for our Great American Beef Herd to grow again.”

The average price of 100 percent ground beef per pound in the U.S. is roughly $6.89, according to U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data shared by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

The president planned a similar move in May, according to Politico, but shelved the idea after pushback from his inner circle.

data.title: The FDA cannot inspect its way to a safe global food supply
data.description:
Two major outbreaks involving imported produce have again tested Americans’ confidence in the safety of their food. A multistate cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce from central Mexico sickened 9,481 people. A salmonella outbreak linked to jalapeño peppers from Sinaloa has sickened 345 people and triggered numerous downstream recalls.

In a country divided on nearly everything, there should be nothing controversial about this: Americans deserve safe food, regardless of where it is produced. The question is how best to ensure it. 

Americans expect fresh fruits, vegetables and seafood year-round. Meeting that demand requires importing enormous quantities of food through increasingly complex global supply chains. Our food-safety system needs to adapt. 

One longstanding element of the Food and Drug Administration’s imported-food safety strategy relies on a surprisingly old-fashioned approach: sending American investigators around the world to inspect individual foreign food-processing facilities. It is the regulatory equivalent of the Lone Ranger riding into town to handle the problem himself. It is also wildly ineffective.

Congress reinforced that approach with the Food Safety Modernization Act. The foreign-inspection target eventually reached 19,200 facilities annually — a level the FDA itself has called unrealistic and unachievable. The agency has proven itself right many times over.

According to a 2025 Government Accountability Office report, the FDA averaged just 917 foreign food-safety inspections annually from fiscal 2018 through 2023 — less than 5 percent of its target. Even in 2019, when the agency conducted 1,727 inspections, it reached only about 9 percent of the target. 

The predictable response is to call for more inspectors, more money and more inspections. But that misses the larger problem. The FDA is relying too heavily on a model that no amount of additional staffing can make scalable.

Imports account for about 15 percent of the U.S. food supply, including 32 percent of fresh vegetables, 55 percent of fresh fruit and 94 percent of seafood. That food comes from more than 200 countries and territories and roughly 125,000 foreign food facilities, plus farms. 

Foreign inspections are not the FDA’s only defense. The agency also relies on importer requirements such as the Foreign Supplier Verification Program, along with border screening, examinations, sampling, testing, import alerts and enforcement. Yet Congress continues to emphasize an inspection target bearing little relation to what the FDA can realistically accomplish.

There is another model worth examining. The European Union places substantial reliance on exporting countries and their “competent authorities,” combined with European oversight and risk-based border controls. For many imported foods, exporting countries must demonstrate that their production and control systems comply with EU requirements. Official certificates are issued by the exporting country’s competent authority. 

European authorities use audits and other oversight to evaluate national control systems, while border controls provide another layer of protection. The central question is broader than whether one processor complied on the day of an inspection: Does the country’s food-safety control system work?

That is fundamentally different from sending an American investigator overseas primarily to determine whether a single processor complies with U.S. requirements. The U.S. need not copy the European system, but its central principle deserves consideration.

The FDA already recognizes this principle. Its Systems Recognition program evaluates whether other countries operate a comparable food-safety regulatory system and allows the FDA and its foreign counterparts to leverage one another’s regulatory systems and redirect resources based on risk. Yet the FDA currently has Systems Recognition arrangements only with Australia, Canada and New Zealand — countries that already have robust food-safety systems. 

Those arrangements can conserve agency resources, but they do relatively little to address the more difficult challenge: ensuring the safety of food coming from major exporting countries where regulatory capacity or compliance may require greater FDA attention. 

That is where the greater opportunity lies. The FDA should work with competent authorities in major food-exporting countries to identify weaknesses and strengthen their ability to oversee the farms and processors supplying the U.S. market. 

The FDA has already demonstrated how such collaboration can work. In August 2023, it established its first Regulatory Partnership Arrangement with Ecuador for aquacultured shrimp exported to the U.S. The arrangement is designed to leverage Ecuador’s commodity-specific regulatory oversight and allow the governments to exchange information, including inspection records and sampling findings. 

That approach should be expanded. 

Importantly, the FDA itself is now moving in this direction. Its 2026 Human Foods Program priorities explicitly call for the agency to “leverage foreign competent authorities” responsible for food offered for import into the United States. The FDA identifies the Food Safety Partnership with Mexico, Regulatory Partnership Arrangements and Systems Recognition as priorities. For imported shrimp, the FDA says it will advance regulatory partnerships with leading shrimp-exporting countries such as India. 

The partnership with Mexico is particularly relevant to the current produce outbreaks. The FDA’s Food Safety Partnership with Mexican agencies grew out of a produce-safety partnership established in 2014 and was expanded in 2020 to cover all FDA-regulated human food. The FDA says that roughly one-third of FDA-regulated human food imported into the U.S. comes from Mexico, including 60 percent of U.S. fresh-produce imports.

Direct FDA inspections remain an important tool, but they should be targeted where they provide the greatest value: high-risk foods, weaker regulatory systems, facilities with poor compliance histories, emerging hazards and verification that foreign authorities are doing their jobs.

For countries with developing food-safety systems, the FDA should combine oversight with technical assistance, training and capacity building. And where governments cannot or will not provide adequate oversight, the FDA should retain its full arsenal of inspections, border examinations, sampling, import alerts and enforcement. 

Congress and the FDA should rethink a foreign-inspection strategy built around a numerical target that the FDA itself says is unrealistic. The objective should not be maximizing the number of American inspectors sent overseas but maximizing protection for American consumers. 

Brett Koonse worked at the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for 31 years as a food-safety official and founded All Things Seafood, LLC.
